authn-vs-authz.proof: An access decision function that first proves identity, then checks permission, and denies with the correct reason when either fails.
authn-vs-authz.unlock: You can state, for any request, which failure is a 401 (not authenticated) and which is a 403 (authenticated but not allowed).
authn-vs-authz.outcome: Separate authentication (who you are) from authorization (what you may do), and enforce both as two distinct checks on every protected action.
authn-vs-authz.doNotClaim: Don't claim a logged-in user is an authorized user — authentication is the door, authorization is the room, and confusing them is how a normal user reaches an admin action.

authn-vs-authz.text: A support agent opens a URL meant for admins and successfully triggers a refund. The app checked that they were logged in — and stopped there. Nobody ran the second check: is THIS user allowed to do THIS thing? This lesson makes authentication and authorization two separate, non-skippable gates.

Every protected endpoint answers two questions in order. AuthN: is this request from a real, verified principal (a valid session or token)? AuthZ: is that principal permitted to perform this specific action on this specific resource? They fail differently — an unauthenticated request is a 401, an authenticated-but-forbidden request is a 403 — and they live in different layers. Collapse them into "if (loggedIn)" and you ship privilege-escalation bugs.

authn-vs-authz.prompt: Before reading: a valid user session hits DELETE /invoices/42, but invoice 42 belongs to a different account. Is that a 401 or a 403, and why?
authn-vs-authz.reveal: A 403. The user IS authenticated (we know who they are — that is why it is not a 401), but they are NOT authorized to delete another account's invoice. 401 = "I don't know who you are"; 403 = "I know who you are and the answer is no." Returning 401 here would wrongly imply re-logging-in could help.

authn-vs-authz.intro: One access decision that runs authentication first, then authorization, and reports which gate failed.
steps: AuthN runs first: no verified principal → 401, and you stop. Authorization never runs for an unknown caller.
AuthZ runs second, on the resource: ownership or an admin role gates the action.
The two failures carry different status codes (401 vs 403) so clients and logs can tell them apart.
The decision takes the resource owner as input — authorization is about THIS resource, not a global flag.
authn-vs-authz.commonMistake: Writing `if (session) allow()` and treating "has a session" as "may do it". That passes authentication and silently skips authorization — any logged-in user can then act on resources they do not own.

authn-vs-authz.text: AUTHENTICATION (authN) establishes WHO is making the request — it verifies a credential (a session cookie, a signed token) and yields a principal, or nothing. AUTHORIZATION (authZ) decides WHAT that principal may do — it evaluates the principal against a policy and the specific resource. They are strictly ordered: you cannot authorize an unknown caller, so authN comes first and, if it fails, you return 401 and never reach authZ. If authN succeeds but the policy says no, you return 403 — the caller is known and simply not permitted; re-authenticating will not help, which is exactly what 403 (vs 401) communicates. The dangerous shortcut is treating presence-of-session as permission: that answers only the first question. Real authorization is per-action and per-resource (owner? admin? in the right account?), which is why the decision must take the resource, not just the user. Keep them separate and every endpoint gets both gates; merge them and you ship the "logged-in therefore allowed" class of bug.
authn-vs-authz.title: Two gates in order: prove identity, then check permission

storyboard.say: Every protected endpoint starts here: an incoming request arrives and must clear two gates before touching anything real.
Gate one is authentication — before anything else, the system asks a single question: who are you?
If no valid session or token resolves to a principal, authN fails and we return 401 — we never even reach the second gate.
Only a verified principal passes through. Now, and only now, do we hand off to gate two: authorization.
AuthZ asks a different question: is THIS known user allowed to do THIS action on THIS resource? If policy says no, it's 403.
If the policy permits it, the principal finally reaches the protected resource and the action goes through.
The trap: treating a valid session as permission. That skips gate two — how a support agent logged in and triggered an admin refund.
Two gates, strictly ordered: 401 means we don't know you, 403 means we know you and you're still not allowed — re-login won't help.

sessions-vs-jwt.proof: A revocation check that instantly kills a server session by ID, and shows why an unexpired JWT keeps validating until it expires.
sessions-vs-jwt.unlock: You can explain why a stateful session is revocable on demand but a stateless JWT is valid until exp unless you add a denylist.
sessions-vs-jwt.outcome: Choose between a server-side session and a self-contained JWT by reasoning about where the state lives and how revocation works.
sessions-vs-jwt.doNotClaim: Don't claim JWTs are 'more secure' by default — they trade instant revocation for statelessness, and that trade is the whole decision.

sessions-vs-jwt.text: Security asks you to log out a compromised account NOW. With server sessions it is one row delete. But the app issues long-lived JWTs, and the stolen token keeps working for its full lifetime because nothing checks a central store. This lesson makes the state-and-revocation trade-off explicit so you pick the right tool.

Both approaches answer "is this request authenticated?" but store the truth in different places. A SERVER SESSION keeps state server-side (a session record) and hands the client an opaque ID in a cookie; the server looks it up each request. A JWT is SELF-CONTAINED: the claims (user, exp, roles) travel in a signed token, so the server verifies the signature without a lookup. Statelessness scales and avoids a per-request read; the cost is revocation — you cannot "un-issue" a valid JWT before its exp without adding a denylist that reintroduces state.

sessions-vs-jwt.prompt: Before reading: you must force-logout a user immediately. Which is one operation with server sessions, and what extra machinery does a plain JWT need to match it?
sessions-vs-jwt.reveal: With server sessions: delete the session record — the next request fails the lookup, instantly logged out. With a plain JWT: nothing to delete; it stays valid until exp. To revoke early you must add a server-side denylist (or short expiries + refresh tokens) — which reintroduces the very per-request state JWTs were meant to avoid.

sessions-vs-jwt.intro: Two verifiers side by side: the session one consults a store (revocable); the JWT one only checks signature + exp (not revocable alone).
steps: Session verify does a store lookup — deleting the record revokes instantly.
JWT verify checks the signature and exp only; there is no store to consult.
Therefore a stolen-but-unexpired JWT keeps validating unless you add a denylist.
The knob for JWTs is exp: short expiries limit the damage window (with refresh tokens to re-issue).
sessions-vs-jwt.commonMistake: Issuing long-lived JWTs and assuming "logout" invalidates them. Clearing the client cookie hides the token locally, but the signed token itself stays valid until exp — a copied token still works.

sessions-vs-jwt.text: The single distinction is state location. A SERVER-SIDE SESSION stores the source of truth on the server (a session table or cache) and gives the browser only an opaque, random session ID in a cookie. Every request costs a lookup, but that lookup is also your control point: delete the record and the user is revoked immediately. A JWT (JSON Web Token) is stateless: the signed token itself carries the claims (sub, exp, roles), so verification is just "is the signature valid and is now < exp?" — no lookup, which scales beautifully and works across services that share only the verify key. The price is revocation: because nothing central is consulted, you cannot invalidate a still-valid JWT on demand. To get revocation back you either keep expiries short and pair with refresh tokens, or maintain a denylist of revoked token IDs — and a denylist is a per-request store lookup, i.e. you have partially re-become stateful. So the real decision is: do you need instant, per-user revocation and easy central control (sessions), or stateless horizontal scale and no shared store (JWT, accepting a bounded validity window)? Neither is "more secure"; they optimize different axes.

storyboard.say: Every request starts here: the browser needs to prove it is authenticated, and there are two ways to carry that proof.
Path one: the client sends an opaque session id in a cookie, and the server takes that id to verify who you are.
The server can't trust the cookie alone, so it looks the id up in the session store on every single request.
That lookup is the control point: delete the row in the store and the user is revoked instantly.
Path two: the client sends a self-contained bearer JWT, and the server just checks the signature and the expiry.
No store lookup means it scales beautifully, but nothing central is consulted, so a stolen token stays valid until it expires.
To revoke a JWT early you must add a denylist the verifier checks, which quietly reintroduces the very state you removed.
The single distinction is state location: sessions keep truth on the server and revoke on delete; JWTs carry truth in the token and pay for it at revocation.

password-storage-oauth.proof: A salted-hash verifier that accepts the right password, rejects the wrong one, and shows two users with the SAME password get DIFFERENT stored hashes.
password-storage-oauth.unlock: You can explain why unique per-user salts defeat precomputed (rainbow) attacks and why the hash must be deliberately slow.
password-storage-oauth.outcome: Store passwords with a salted, slow hash so a database leak does not reveal passwords, and know when to delegate login to OAuth instead.
password-storage-oauth.doNotClaim: Don't claim SHA-256 alone is password hashing — a fast, unsalted hash is crackable at billions/sec and shares hashes across identical passwords.

password-storage-oauth.text: A database dump leaks. If passwords were stored as plaintext or a fast unsalted hash, every account is compromised in minutes — and because users reuse passwords, so are their other accounts. This lesson builds storage that stays safe even after the DB is stolen, and shows when to not store passwords at all (OAuth).

Passwords must be stored so that possessing the database does not reveal them. The rules: never plaintext; never a fast general-purpose hash (SHA-256/MD5) which GPUs crack at billions/sec; use a SLOW, SALTED password hash (bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2, PBKDF2). A per-user random SALT makes identical passwords hash differently (killing rainbow tables and cross-account reuse), and the deliberate slowness makes brute force expensive. OAuth is the alternative: delegate authentication to a provider (Google/GitHub) so you never store a password at all — you store an account link instead.

password-storage-oauth.prompt: Before reading: two users pick the password "hunter2". With a correct scheme, are their stored hashes the same or different — and why does that matter?
password-storage-oauth.reveal: Different — because each gets a unique random salt that is hashed together with the password. That means an attacker cannot tell the two users share a password, cannot reuse one crack against the other, and cannot use a precomputed rainbow table. Identical stored hashes (unsalted) would leak all of that at once.

password-storage-oauth.intro: A salted, iterated hash (PBKDF2 stands in for bcrypt/Argon2 here) with per-user salts, plus constant-time verification.
steps: Generate a unique random salt per user and store it alongside the hash.
Hash password+salt with many iterations (slow on purpose) — never a single fast hash.
Store salt + hash, never the password; the password is unrecoverable by design.
Verify by re-hashing the input with the stored salt and comparing in constant time.
password-storage-oauth.commonMistake: Using `sha256(password)` with no salt. It is fast (crackable at scale) and unsalted (identical passwords share a hash, so one crack breaks many accounts and rainbow tables apply).

password-storage-oauth.text: A password store must survive theft of the database. Two properties get you there. SALTING: mix a unique, random per-user salt into the hash input, so the same password produces different stored hashes for different users. This defeats rainbow tables (precomputed hash→password maps are useless when every hash is individually salted) and hides password reuse across accounts. SLOWNESS (work factor): use an algorithm designed to be deliberately expensive — bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2, or PBKDF2 with a high iteration count — so an attacker who steals the hashes can only test a few thousand guesses per second instead of billions. A plain SHA-256 fails both: it is unsalted by itself and far too fast. You store the salt and the hash (the salt is not secret — it just needs to be unique), never the password, and you verify by re-hashing the attempt with the stored salt and comparing in constant time (timingSafeEqual) so you do not leak match progress via timing. OAuth sidesteps the whole problem: you delegate the credential check to an identity provider and store only a link to their account — no password to hash, leak, or reset, at the cost of depending on that provider and handling their tokens.

To log a user in, we re-hash their attempt with the stored salt and compare in constant time to avoid timing leaks.
Unique salt kills rainbow tables and hides reuse; slow hashing survives theft. The database dump becomes worthless.

protecting-routes-server-side.proof: A middleware chain that short-circuits unauthenticated/forbidden requests and only reaches the handler when both gates pass.
protecting-routes-server-side.unlock: You can explain why route protection must run server-side in a middleware layer, not in the client or scattered inside handlers.
protecting-routes-server-side.outcome: Guard protected routes with server-side middleware that runs before the handler, so no protected handler executes for an unauthenticated or unauthorized request.
protecting-routes-server-side.doNotClaim: Don't claim a hidden link protects a route — the endpoint is directly callable, so the guard must live on the server in front of the handler.

protecting-routes-server-side.text: A "protected" dashboard route is safe in the UI (the nav link is hidden) but a user pastes the API URL and gets full data back. The protection was cosmetic. This lesson puts a real guard in the request pipeline so the handler never runs without passing the gates from lesson 1.

Route protection is where authN + authZ get ENFORCED on every request. The pattern is a middleware chain: small functions that run in order before the handler, each able to short-circuit with a response. requireAuth attaches the principal or returns 401; requireRole(...) checks permission or returns 403; only if both pass does the actual handler run. Because it sits in the server pipeline, it cannot be bypassed by the client — unlike hiding a button, which only affects what the honest UI shows.

protecting-routes-server-side.prompt: Before reading: your React app hides the "Admin" link for non-admins. Is the admin API route protected? Why or why not?
protecting-routes-server-side.reveal: No. Hiding the link only changes the UI; the API route is still directly reachable with curl/fetch. Protection must be enforced on the SERVER, in front of the handler (middleware), so that a crafted request without a valid session/role is rejected before any handler logic runs.

protecting-routes-server-side.intro: A tiny middleware chain: authenticate, then authorize, then handle — each step can stop the chain.
steps: Each middleware returns null to continue or a response to short-circuit.
requireAuth runs first (401 stops the chain); requireRole runs next (403 stops it).
The handler executes ONLY after every guard passed — protection is not inside the handler.

protecting-routes-server-side.commonMistake: Putting the auth check inside the handler after some work has already happened (a DB read, a log write). A guard must run BEFORE the handler; a check buried mid-handler can be skipped by another code path.

protecting-routes-server-side.text: Protecting a route means guaranteeing that the handler cannot run unless the request passed the gates. The clean way is a MIDDLEWARE CHAIN: an ordered list of small functions that execute before the handler, each with the power to short-circuit and return a response. A typical chain is requireAuth → requireRole("admin") → handler: the first attaches/validates the principal and returns 401 if absent; the second checks permission and returns 403 if denied; only when none short-circuit does the handler run. Three properties make this correct. It runs SERVER-SIDE, so it applies to every caller including curl — client-side hiding is UX, not security. It runs BEFORE the handler, so no protected logic executes for a rejected request (no partial work, no data leak). And it is CENTRALIZED and composable, so you attach the same guards to many routes instead of re-implementing checks (and forgetting one) in each handler. This is exactly how Express middleware, Next.js middleware, and framework "guards" work; the mechanism is a chain that can stop early.

storyboard.say: Every request to a protected route enters the middleware chain here, before any handler logic gets a chance to run.

Only an authenticated request passes forward to the second gate, requireRole, which checks permission.
Authenticated but not authorized? requireRole short-circuits with a 403 denial. Authentication is not the same as permission.
Only when both gates pass does control reach the actual route handler and return real data.
The insight: guarding in the server pipeline guarantees the handler cannot run unguarded. Hiding a nav link is UX; this is security.

stripe-object-model.text: A "change the monthly price" ticket turns into a bug hunt because amounts are hardcoded in the app and duplicated across three files. Stripe already models this: the amount lives on a Price object you reference by id. This lesson makes the customer/product/price model explicit so pricing lives in Stripe, not scattered in code.

Stripe's billing is four core objects. A PRODUCT is the thing you sell ("Pro plan"). A PRICE belongs to a product and defines currency + unit_amount (in the smallest currency unit, e.g. cents) and, for recurring billing, an interval (month/year). A CUSTOMER represents the buyer and owns their subscriptions and invoices. A SUBSCRIPTION links a customer to one or more prices and bills on the interval. You reference a price by id (price_...) — you never hardcode the amount — so changing pricing is a Stripe change, not a deploy.

A product is the item; each distinct amount+interval is its own Price. Your checkout/subscription references the specific price id the customer chose — the product just groups them.

stripe-object-model.intro: Resolve a customer's subscription to its price and product, and compute the charge — refusing a price that does not belong to the product.
steps: A subscription references a price id; the price references a product id — follow the chain.
unit_amount is in cents; a USD 15/month plan is unit_amount: 1500.
Never read a hardcoded amount — read the Price the customer is actually on.
A price whose product does not exist is a data error; refuse it rather than charge blindly.
stripe-object-model.commonMistake: Hardcoding the dollar amount in the app instead of reading it from the Price object. When pricing changes in Stripe, your app now charges the old (wrong) number and the two silently disagree.

stripe-object-model.text: Stripe separates WHAT you sell from HOW MUCH and HOW OFTEN. A PRODUCT ("Pro plan", "Team seat") is a stable catalog entry. A PRICE belongs to exactly one product and pins down the money: a currency, a unit_amount in the smallest currency unit (1500 = USD 15.00/month), and, for recurring products, an interval (month or year). Because one product can have many prices (monthly vs annual, USD vs EUR, promotional tiers), you always transact against a specific PRICE id (price_...), never a bare number in your code. A CUSTOMER (cus_...) is the buyer record that owns payment methods, invoices, and subscriptions; a SUBSCRIPTION ties a customer to one or more prices and generates invoices each interval. The practical payoff: pricing changes happen in Stripe (add a new Price, point checkout at its id), not in a code deploy — and your app resolves the truth by following customer → subscription → price → product, reading unit_amount from the Price rather than trusting a constant that will drift.

Each interval the Subscription generates an Invoice, billing the customer automatically off that referenced Price.
The insight: Stripe splits what you sell from how much and how often, so a price change edits one Price object, not hardcoded amounts in three files.

hosted-checkout.text: A team is about to hand-roll a card form to "save a redirect," and just walked into PCI scope and a security review. Stripe hosts the whole payment page for you. This lesson builds a Checkout Session correctly — the price, the mode, and the return URLs — and hands the customer to Stripe.

Hosted Checkout is Stripe's recommended path: you create a Checkout Session server-side with line_items (each referencing a price id and quantity), a mode (payment for one-time, subscription for recurring, setup to save a card), and success_url + cancel_url; you then redirect the customer to session.url. Stripe renders the payment page, collects the card, handles SCA, and sends the customer back. The mode MUST match the price: a recurring price requires mode: subscription; using mode: payment with it is an error.

hosted-checkout.prompt: Before reading: you pass a recurring (monthly) price to a Checkout Session with mode: "payment". What is wrong?
hosted-checkout.reveal: mode must match the price type. A recurring price needs mode: "subscription" — it creates an ongoing subscription. mode: "payment" is for one-time charges and rejects a recurring price. Pick the mode from the price's type before you create the session.

hosted-checkout.text: Hosted Checkout inverts who owns the risky part. Server-side, you create a CHECKOUT SESSION describing the purchase: line_items (each a { price, quantity } referencing a real price id), a mode that selects the billing behavior (payment = one-time charge, subscription = recurring, setup = save a card for later), and the two return URLs — success_url (where Stripe sends a completed customer, optionally templated with {CHECKOUT_SESSION_ID}) and cancel_url (where an abandoning customer lands). You then redirect the browser to session.url. From there STRIPE renders the payment page, collects and validates the card, runs any Strong Customer Authentication, and processes the charge — the card data goes browser→Stripe and never touches your server, which is what keeps you out of heavy PCI scope. The one correctness rule to internalize: mode must agree with the price. A recurring price demands mode: subscription; a one-time price demands mode: payment. Get that pairing wrong and Stripe rejects the session, because mode is what tells Stripe whether it is starting a subscription or taking a single payment.

Stripe now owns the risky part: it renders the payment page, collects the card, and runs Strong Customer Authentication.
If the charge completes, Stripe sends the customer to your success_url, optionally templated with the checkout session id.
If they abandon the page, Stripe returns them to your cancel_url — a clean exit, not a dead end.
The insight: Hosted Checkout inverts ownership — you describe the purchase, Stripe touches the card, and both outcomes route back to you.

This lesson makes the return flow trustworthy: confirm the outcome from Stripe, never from the URL the browser landed on.

Checkout ends by redirecting the customer to success_url (completed) or cancel_url (abandoned). These are UX signals, not authoritative outcomes: a user can bookmark, refresh, or share the success URL, and a redirect can arrive before Stripe finishes processing. So on success_url you RETRIEVE the session server-side (via the {CHECKOUT_SESSION_ID}) and check its payment_status / status before granting anything; the authoritative confirmation is the webhook (Module 3). cancel_url means the customer backed out — grant nothing, offer to try again.

You guarantee it by NOT granting from the redirect itself: retrieve the session server-side, check payment_status === "paid", and make the grant idempotent (keyed on the session/subscription) so reloads do not re-grant. The redirect is not a payment event.

success-cancel-flow.text: Checkout's two return URLs are for the human, not for your ledger. Landing on success_url means "the customer finished the flow in their browser" — it does NOT mean the payment is confirmed, because that URL is a plain page the user can refresh, bookmark, or open before Stripe has finished, and nothing about a GET request proves money moved. So treat success as PROVISIONAL: use the {CHECKOUT_SESSION_ID} embedded in success_url to RETRIEVE the Checkout Session server-side and inspect its payment_status (or status) — only "paid"/"complete" justifies granting anything. Make that grant IDEMPOTENT (keyed on the session id or resulting subscription) so repeated visits do not stack free access. cancel_url is the easy case: the customer abandoned, so you grant nothing and invite them to retry. The fully authoritative confirmation is not even the retrieve — it is the webhook Stripe sends (checkout.session.completed), which is the subject of Module 3. The discipline: the browser tells you where the user went; Stripe tells you what actually happened.

storyboard.say: Checkout finishes and Stripe redirects the customer's browser to your success_url — a plain page they just landed on.
That redirect is only a UX signal: the user can refresh, bookmark, or replay it, and nothing about a GET request proves money moved.
So treat success as provisional. Read the CHECKOUT_SESSION_ID from the URL and retrieve the session from Stripe, server-side.
The retrieved session carries the authoritative status — this is the fact you check, not the URL the browser landed on.
Decision point: only payment_status paid or complete justifies granting anything.

The payment happened; your app just never heard about it from a reliable channel. This lesson moves fulfillment onto the webhook, the one signal that arrives even when the browser does not.

The client redirect (success_url) is best-effort: the user may close the tab, lose connectivity, or the page may load before processing finishes — so it cannot be your fulfillment trigger. Stripe instead sends a WEBHOOK: a server-to-server HTTP POST to your endpoint carrying an Event object (e.g. checkout.session.completed, invoice.payment_succeeded) the moment something happens. Because it is server-to-server and retried until you 2xx, it arrives reliably regardless of the browser. The rule: read/confirm on redirect for UX, but GRANT/FULFILL on the verified webhook.

webhooks-source-of-truth.text: There are two channels that tell you a checkout finished, and they are not equally trustworthy. The CLIENT REDIRECT (success_url) depends on the customer's browser completing a navigation — it can be interrupted by a closed tab, a crash, lost connectivity, or simply never happen, and a URL can be replayed or forged. The WEBHOOK is a server-to-server HTTP POST from Stripe to an endpoint you register, carrying an Event object that describes exactly what happened (checkout.session.completed, invoice.payment_succeeded, customer.subscription.updated, and so on). It is delivered independently of any browser and is RETRIED on a schedule until your endpoint returns a 2xx acknowledgement, so it is the durable, at-least-once signal. Therefore fulfillment — granting access, provisioning, recording the sale — hangs off the verified webhook event, while the redirect is demoted to a UX nicety ("Thanks, you're all set!"). Your endpoint's job is narrow: verify the event is really from Stripe (next lesson), do the fulfillment work idempotently, and return 2xx promptly so Stripe stops retrying. This is the inversion beginners miss: the customer's browser is a hint; Stripe's webhook is the truth.

verifying-webhook-signatures.proof: A verifier that ACCEPTS a genuinely-signed payload and REJECTS a tampered payload and an out-of-tolerance timestamp — with the HMAC actually computed via Node crypto.

verifying-webhook-signatures.text: Your webhook endpoint is a public URL. Anyone can POST a forged "payment succeeded" event and get free access — unless every event is cryptographically proven to come from Stripe. This lesson has you compute the exact HMAC Stripe computes, compare it safely, and reject forgeries and replays.

Because a webhook endpoint is publicly reachable, Stripe signs every event. The Stripe-Signature header looks like t=timestamp,v1=signature,v0=signature. To verify, you reconstruct the signed_payload by concatenating the timestamp, a period (.), and the RAW request body, compute HMAC-SHA256 of that string keyed by your endpoint signing secret (whsec_...), and compare the hex digest to v1 using a constant-time comparison. You also check the timestamp is within a tolerance (Stripe defaults to 300 seconds) to prevent replay of an old, valid event.

The key is your endpoint signing secret (whsec_...). You compare the resulting hex digest to the v1 value in the Stripe-Signature header, in constant time — and reject if the timestamp is outside your tolerance (default 300s).

steps: Parse the header into t (timestamp) and v1 (signature).
Reject immediately if the timestamp is outside the tolerance window (replay defense).
Reconstruct signed_payload = `${t}.${rawBody}` using the RAW body, then HMAC-SHA256 it with the signing secret.
Compare your hex digest to v1 in constant time (timingSafeEqual); any mismatch is a forgery.
verifying-webhook-signatures.commonMistake: Verifying against a re-serialized JSON body (JSON.parse then JSON.stringify) instead of the raw bytes. Re-serialization changes whitespace/key order, so the HMAC no longer matches — you must sign the exact raw body Stripe sent.

verifying-webhook-signatures.text: A webhook signature proves two things: the event really came from someone holding your signing secret (authenticity) and it was not altered in transit (integrity). Stripe attaches a Stripe-Signature header of the form t=<unix-timestamp>,v1=<hex>,v0=<hex>. Verification is a recomputation you do yourself: build the SIGNED_PAYLOAD by concatenating the timestamp string, a literal period, and the RAW request body exactly as received (bytes untouched — do not parse and re-stringify, which would change whitespace and break the match); compute HMAC-SHA256 of that payload using your endpoint's signing secret (whsec_...) as the key; and compare the resulting hex digest against the header's v1 value. The comparison MUST be constant-time (crypto.timingSafeEqual) so an attacker cannot learn the correct signature byte-by-byte from timing. On top of authenticity you defend against REPLAY: reject any event whose timestamp is outside a tolerance window (Stripe's libraries default to 300 seconds), so a captured-but-valid old event cannot be resent later. If either check fails, respond 400 and do nothing. In production stripe.webhooks.constructEvent does all of this for you — but you must feed it the raw body, and understanding the mechanism is what lets you debug the "signature verification failed" that every integration hits.

storyboard.say: A request lands with a Stripe-Signature header shaped like t=timestamp,v1=hex — we parse the timestamp out first.
If that timestamp is stale, someone may be replaying an old captured event, so we reject it with a 400.
When the timestamp is fresh, we rebuild the signed_payload: the timestamp, a literal period, then the raw request body untouched.
We compute HMAC-SHA256 over that exact string, keyed by our endpoint signing secret whsec_..., producing our own hex digest.
That digest goes into a constant-time compare against the header's v1 value — timing-safe so attackers learn nothing from response speed.
If the digests differ, the event was forged or altered in transit, so we reject it with a 400 and never trust it.
The insight: only a holder of your secret can recompute this digest, proving authenticity and integrity on a public URL.

idempotent-handlers.text: A brief timeout makes Stripe redeliver a payment event, and your handler grants a second month / sends a second shipment / emails a second receipt. The delivery guarantee is at-least-once; without dedup, every retry is a duplicate side effect. This lesson makes the handler idempotent using the event id.

Stripe delivers events AT-LEAST-ONCE: if your endpoint is slow, errors, or a network blip drops the ack, Stripe retries the SAME event (same event id, evt_...). That means your handler may see an event two or more times. Idempotency is the fix: before doing work, check whether you have already processed this event id; if so, skip and just ack; if not, do the work and record the id — ideally in the same transaction as the side effect. The event id is the natural idempotency key.

idempotent-handlers.reveal: Exactly one. You guarantee it with an idempotency ledger keyed on the event id: on first arrival you grant and record evt_...; on the second and third you see the id already recorded and skip the grant (still returning 2xx). The work happens once; the extra deliveries are acknowledged but do nothing.

Every delivery returns 2xx — a duplicate is a no-op, not an error.
idempotent-handlers.commonMistake: Recording the event id BEFORE the work completes (or in a separate transaction). If the work then fails, the id is marked processed and the retry is skipped — the side effect never happened. Record the id atomically with the effect.

idempotent-handlers.text: Webhook delivery is AT-LEAST-ONCE, not exactly-once: Stripe retries an event until it receives a 2xx, and a slow handler, a transient error, or a dropped acknowledgement can cause the SAME event (identical event id) to be delivered multiple times. Any handler with a side effect — granting access, shipping, charging, emailing — must therefore be IDEMPOTENT: running it twice with the same event must have the same result as running it once. The standard technique is an idempotency ledger keyed on the event id. On each event you first check whether that id is already recorded; if yes, you skip the work and simply acknowledge; if no, you perform the side effect and record the id. The subtle correctness point is ATOMICITY: record the id together with the side effect (same database transaction), so you never end up in the two failure states — recorded-but-not-done (a real retry gets wrongly skipped) or done-but-not-recorded (a retry re-does the work). Because event ids are stable across redeliveries, this ledger turns Stripe's at-least-once guarantee into the exactly-once behavior your business logic needs. Note this is distinct from the idempotency KEY you send on outbound API requests — here you are deduping inbound events by their id.

reconciling-state.text: Your app thinks a user is active; Stripe canceled them last week because a webhook was missed during an outage. Now they have access they are not paying for. This lesson models local state as a projection of Stripe events and adds reconciliation so a missed event self-heals instead of silently drifting.

Your database holds a LOCAL copy of subscription state (active, past_due, canceled) so you can gate features without calling Stripe on every request. That copy is a PROJECTION built by applying webhook events as a state machine: checkout.session.completed / invoice.payment_succeeded → active; invoice.payment_failed → past_due; customer.subscription.deleted → canceled. But webhooks can be missed (outage, bug), so the projection can DRIFT. Reconciliation fixes it: periodically (or on suspicion) fetch the subscription from Stripe and overwrite local state, because Stripe is authoritative.

They diverged because an event (customer.subscription.deleted or a failed payment leading to cancellation) was missed or not applied. The fix is reconciliation: fetch the subscription from Stripe and overwrite local state to match, then investigate the missed event.

reconciling-state.commonMistake: Treating the local database as the source of truth and never reconciling. One missed webhook and the projection drifts forever — a canceled customer keeps access, or an active one is wrongly locked out.

reconciling-state.text: You keep a LOCAL subscription state so feature-gating is a cheap database read instead of a Stripe API call per request. Crucially, that local state is not the truth — it is a PROJECTION derived by applying Stripe's events through a state machine. Each relevant event is a transition: a successful checkout or paid invoice moves the subscription to active; a failed invoice payment moves it to past_due; a subscription deletion moves it to canceled; everything else leaves state untouched. Fold the ordered event stream through those transitions and you get the current local state. The catch is that webhooks are deliverable-but-not-guaranteed-forever: during an outage or a handler bug an event can be missed, and once you miss a transition your projection DRIFTS from Stripe. That is why you add RECONCILIATION: on a schedule, or whenever you suspect divergence (a support ticket, a mismatch), you fetch the subscription's current status directly from Stripe and OVERWRITE your local copy, because Stripe is the authoritative system of record and your database is a cache of it. The mental model — events as transitions, local state as a projection, Stripe as the tiebreaker — is exactly how robust billing systems stay correct despite imperfect delivery.

subscription-lifecycle.text: Your gate does `status === "active"` and locks out every trialing user on day one — and separately keeps letting a past_due user in for months. The status field has more than two values, each with a meaning. This lesson maps the real lifecycle to an access decision you can defend.

A Stripe subscription's status is one of a fixed set: incomplete, incomplete_expired, trialing, active, past_due, canceled, unpaid, or paused. incomplete means the first payment has not succeeded yet (it becomes active on payment, or incomplete_expired if unpaid within ~23 hours). trialing is a free trial (access, no payment yet). active is paid and current. past_due means a renewal payment failed and retries are underway (a grace period). canceled/unpaid mean access should end. Your access policy decides which statuses grant access.

The point: it is not a simple active-or-nothing check; each status has a defined meaning you gate on.

subscription-lifecycle.text: A subscription is a small lifecycle, and its status field names where it is. The real values are incomplete, incomplete_expired, trialing, active, past_due, canceled, unpaid, and paused. Reading them precisely matters because access is a POLICY over these states, not a boolean. incomplete means the initial payment has not gone through yet; it advances to active once paid, or to incomplete_expired if it stays unpaid past Stripe's window (~23 hours). trialing is a live free trial — the customer should have full access even though no charge has occurred. active is the steady, paid-and-current state. past_due is the important nuance: a scheduled renewal payment FAILED and Stripe is retrying, so it is a grace period during which you choose whether to keep access (many products grant a short window to give dunning a chance, then cut off). canceled and unpaid mean billing has ended or given up — block. paused (e.g. a trial that ended without a payment method) does not bill and generally blocks until resumed. The engineering takeaway: enumerate the statuses, decide grant/block for EACH one deliberately, and encode that policy in one function — so trialing users are not locked out and past_due users are not silently comped forever.

storyboard.say: A subscription is a lifecycle, and the status field names where it is. Access must be a policy over these states, not a boolean.
New subscriptions start at incomplete: the first payment has not cleared yet, so no access has been earned.
Once that first charge succeeds, incomplete advances to active, the steady paid-and-current state.
Trialing is a live free trial: no charge yet, but the customer should have full access, then converts to paid active.
Here is the trap: a renewal payment fails and active becomes past_due while Stripe retries the card.
Past_due is a grace window, not a lockout. If a retry succeeds it returns to active with no disruption.
But if retries exhaust, it falls to canceled or unpaid, and only then do you block access.
So grant on trialing and active, keep grace for past_due, block the rest. The field has meaning, not just true or false.

customer-portal.text: Support is drowning in "update my card" and "cancel my plan" tickets, and someone proposes building a whole billing dashboard. Stripe already hosts one. This lesson wires the customer portal — a session scoped to one authenticated customer — so users self-serve and your state updates via webhook.

The Stripe customer portal is a hosted page where customers manage their own billing: update payment methods, view invoices, change or cancel plans. You create a billing_portal.Session for a specific customer id with a return_url, then redirect them to session.url. Every change they make emits webhooks (customer.subscription.updated, customer.subscription.deleted, etc.) that update your local state via the Module 3 machinery. The security-critical part: the session must be bound to the AUTHENTICATED customer — never let a user open a portal for someone else's customer id.

If you let the client supply an arbitrary customer id, a user could open the billing portal for another customer and see/modify their subscription. The session must be scoped to exactly the authenticated customer.

customer-portal.text: The customer portal is Stripe's hosted self-service billing surface: from it a customer can update their payment method, download invoices, switch plans, and cancel — all the operations that otherwise become support tickets and custom UI. You enable it by creating a billing_portal.Session for a SPECIFIC customer id with a return_url, then redirecting the browser to session.url; Stripe renders the management page and returns the customer to your return_url when they are done. Two things make this both easy and safe. First, you build almost no UI — the cancel/update/invoice flows are Stripe's, and whatever the customer changes is emitted as webhooks (customer.subscription.updated when they switch plans, customer.subscription.deleted when they cancel), which flow through your verified, idempotent handler and update the local subscription state you gate on. Second — and this is the security invariant — the portal session must be bound to the AUTHENTICATED customer. The customer id is derived server-side from the logged-in user (your users table maps user → stripe_customer_id); it is NEVER taken from client input, because a portal session grants full billing control over that customer, so accepting an arbitrary id would let one user manage another's subscription. Scope the session to exactly one authenticated customer, and let webhooks reconcile the rest.

plan-changes-proration.text: A customer upgrades on day 15 of a 30-day cycle and gets charged a full new-plan month on top of the one they already paid — an angry ticket and a refund. Stripe prorates by default; you need to understand the math to reason about the invoice. This lesson computes proration from first principles.

When a customer changes plans mid-cycle, PRORATION makes the money fair: they get a CREDIT for the unused portion of the old plan and a CHARGE for the portion of the new plan they will actually use for the rest of the cycle. The driver is the fraction of the billing period remaining. Stripe computes this automatically (proration_behavior defaults to create_prorations) and issues proration line items on the next invoice; understanding the arithmetic lets you predict and display the net amount instead of treating the invoice as magic.

plan-changes-proration.reveal: About USD 10 now: they get a credit for the unused half of the old plan (about USD 5, half of USD 10) and a charge for the remaining half of the new plan (about USD 15, half of USD 30), netting about USD 10 now. Then the USD 30/mo continues at the next renewal. Proration = credit unused old + charge used-forward new, scaled by the remaining-time fraction.

plan-changes-proration.intro: Compute the credit for unused old-plan time and the charge for remaining new-plan time from the remaining fraction.
steps: Compute the remaining-time fraction: daysLeft / daysInPeriod.
Credit = old price × remaining fraction (refund the unused old plan).
Charge = new price × remaining fraction (pay for the rest on the new plan).
Net = charge − credit; a downgrade can make net negative (a credit).
plan-changes-proration.commonMistake: Charging the full new-plan amount on an upgrade with no credit for the time already paid on the old plan. The customer double-pays for the overlap and rightly disputes it.

plan-changes-proration.text: Proration keeps billing fair when a subscription changes mid-cycle. The core quantity is the REMAINING FRACTION of the current billing period: daysLeft / daysInPeriod (Stripe works in seconds, but the ratio is the same idea). On a plan change you compute two prorated line items. A CREDIT for the unused portion of the OLD plan — the customer already paid for the whole period, so the part they will not use is refunded: oldPrice × remainingFraction. And a CHARGE for the portion of the NEW plan they will use for the rest of the period: newPrice × remainingFraction. The immediate net is charge − credit: for an UPGRADE it is positive (they owe the difference for the remaining time), for a DOWNGRADE it is negative (they receive a credit, often applied to future invoices). From the next renewal onward they simply pay the new plan's full price. Stripe does this automatically — proration_behavior defaults to create_prorations, which adds these credit/charge line items to the upcoming invoice — but understanding the arithmetic is what lets you preview "you'll be charged X now" accurately and debug an invoice a customer questions, instead of treating the proration line items as inexplicable.

Scale the old price by that fraction to credit the unused portion they already paid for: oldPrice times remainingFraction.
Scale the new price by the same fraction to charge only the part of the new plan they'll actually use: newPrice times remainingFraction.
Both prorated line items land on the next invoice: subtract the credit, add the charge.
The immediate net is charge minus credit: positive for an upgrade, a credit back for a downgrade. That's fair billing.

failed-payments-dunning.text: A customer's card expires; your app cancels them on the first failed charge and you lose a payer who would have updated their card the next day. Real billing gives failures a retry runway. This lesson models the dunning lifecycle so failures recover when they can and end cleanly when they cannot.

Recurring payments fail routinely (expired cards, insufficient funds). When a renewal invoice fails, Stripe fires invoice.payment_failed and the subscription goes past_due, then Billing RETRIES the invoice on a schedule (Smart Retries) and can send dunning emails prompting the customer to fix their payment method. If a retry succeeds, invoice.payment_succeeded fires and the subscription returns to active. If all retries are exhausted, Stripe applies your configured terminal behavior — cancel the subscription, mark it unpaid, or leave it past_due — which you handle to revoke access.

Each retry either succeeds (→ active, recovered) or fails again. Only after ALL retries are exhausted does Stripe apply your configured terminal action (cancel / mark unpaid). You revoke access on that terminal event, not on the first failure.

failed-payments-dunning.intro: A dunning driver: advance retries, recover on success, apply the terminal action when exhausted.
steps: First failure → past_due, not canceled.
Each scheduled retry either recovers (→ active) or consumes an attempt.
A mid-sequence success stops dunning and restores access.
When retries are exhausted, apply the configured terminal action (cancel/unpaid) and revoke access.
failed-payments-dunning.commonMistake: Revoking access (and treating the customer as churned) on the first invoice.payment_failed. Most failures are transient — you cut off a customer who would have recovered on the very next retry.

failed-payments-dunning.text: Failed recurring payments are normal, and mature billing treats them as a RECOVERABLE lifecycle rather than an immediate loss. The sequence: a renewal invoice fails → Stripe emits invoice.payment_failed and moves the subscription to PAST_DUE → Stripe Billing retries the invoice on a schedule (SMART RETRIES, which time attempts for the best recovery odds) and can send DUNNING emails asking the customer to update their card. Two outcomes branch from there. If any retry succeeds, invoice.payment_succeeded fires and the subscription returns to ACTIVE — the customer never lost access if your past_due grace policy (Module 4, lesson 1) kept them in during the retries. If EVERY retry fails, the dunning process is exhausted and Stripe applies the TERMINAL action you configured: cancel the subscription (status canceled), mark it unpaid (status unpaid, no further attempts), or leave it past_due — and that terminal event is where you finally revoke access. The engineering discipline is to key access changes off the right events: enter a grace state on the first failure, restore on a retry success, and only truly cut off on the terminal exhausted-retries event. Do that and transient declines self-heal while genuinely dead subscriptions end cleanly.

If any retry succeeds, invoice.payment_succeeded fires and the subscription returns to active — a payer recovered instead of lost.
Only when every retry fails does Billing take terminal action — canceled or unpaid — ending the relationship cleanly.
The insight: treat failed payments as a recoverable lifecycle, not an instant loss — the runway saves customers who'd have paid the next day.

Entitlements should be COMPUTED from the subscription, not hand-set. This lesson builds a resolver so what a user can do always follows what they are paying for.

An ENTITLEMENT is the right to use a specific feature. In a subscription product, entitlements are DERIVED: (plan → feature set) combined with (subscription status → access allowed?). A Pro plan maps to {export, api, seats:5}; a Free plan to {export:false,...}. Whether those features are actually granted depends on the status gate from Module 4 (active/trialing grant; canceled blocks). Computing entitlements from the live subscription — rather than caching an is_paid boolean someone edits by hand — is what keeps access and billing in lockstep as customers upgrade, downgrade, lapse, and recover.

entitlements.text: An entitlement is "may this customer use this feature right now?" and the only reliable way to answer it is to DERIVE it from the current subscription rather than store it. The derivation has two inputs. First, the PLAN → FEATURE SET mapping: each plan (Free, Pro, Team) defines exactly which features and limits it includes (export, API access, seat count). Second, the STATUS → ACCESS gate from Module 4: active and trialing grant access, past_due may during a grace window, and canceled/unpaid/incomplete block it. An entitlement check composes them — status must grant access AND the plan must include the feature — so that a Pro customer who has canceled loses everything, and an active Free customer never sees Pro features. The anti-pattern is a stored boolean like is_premium: it is a denormalized copy of the subscription that drifts the instant billing changes (a downgrade nobody propagated, a lapse the webhook missed), silently divorcing access from payment. By computing entitlements from the live subscription state (which your webhooks keep current and reconciliation keeps honest), access follows money automatically: upgrades unlock, downgrades restrict, lapses revoke, recoveries restore — all without a human toggling a flag. This resolver is the join point of the whole course: the auth gates decide WHO, and entitlements decide WHAT, keyed on what they pay for.

That single line drags your entire server into the strictest PCI audit — and stores card data you must never hold. This lesson builds the habit and a linter that keeps card data out of your systems entirely.

PCI DSS governs anyone who handles cardholder data. The winning move is to MINIMIZE SCOPE: if raw card numbers (the PAN) never touch your servers, you qualify for the simplest validation (SAQ A). You achieve that with tokenization — Stripe.js/Elements or hosted Checkout collect the card in the browser and send it directly to Stripe, which returns a token/id (a PaymentMethod or a Checkout Session) that your server handles instead of the card. Your code deals only in ids like pm_... and cus_...; the moment a raw PAN reaches your endpoint, your scope balloons.

The fix is to never receive the PAN at all.

pci-scope.text: PCI DSS applies to any system that stores, processes, or transmits cardholder data, and its requirements scale with how much card data you touch. The strategic goal is SCOPE MINIMIZATION: arrange your integration so the raw card number (PAN) never reaches your servers, which qualifies you for the lightest self-assessment (SAQ A) instead of the heavyweight controls (encryption, network segmentation, penetration testing, formal audits) that apply once a PAN enters your environment. TOKENIZATION is how you get there. With Stripe.js/Elements or hosted Checkout, the card fields live in a Stripe-controlled context in the browser, so the PAN goes DIRECTLY browser→Stripe and never through your backend; Stripe hands back an opaque reference — a PaymentMethod id (pm_...), a Checkout Session, a Customer id — and your server works exclusively with those references. The failure mode to guard against is any code path that receives the actual card number: a "custom form" that POSTs the PAN to your API, a support tool that logs it, a proxy that forwards it. Each one drags your server into the cardholder-data environment and multiplies your compliance burden, even if you never persist the number. The rule is absolute and lintable: raw card data in equals scope expansion; ids/tokens only equals minimal scope. Design so the PAN is Stripe's problem, not yours.

refunds-cancellation.text: You refund an unhappy customer, and they keep full access for another month because nothing revoked their entitlement — the refund only moved money. Reversing a charge and removing access are two actions. This lesson wires both: compute the refund, then revoke on the event.

A REFUND reverses a charge: create a Refund against a PaymentIntent/Charge, omitting amount for a full refund or passing a smaller amount (in the smallest currency unit) for a partial one. Stripe emits charge.refunded. CANCELLATION ends a subscription (status → canceled), emitting customer.subscription.deleted. Neither event, by itself, revokes application access — that is YOUR entitlement logic from earlier this module. So the pattern is: perform the money action (refund/cancel) and, on the resulting webhook, run the access-revocation step. Two separate concerns, both required.

Money reversal and access removal are two separate steps you both own.

refunds-cancellation.text: Ending a paid relationship has two independent halves, and shipping only one is the classic bug. The MONEY half is the refund or cancellation. A REFUND reverses a specific charge: you create a Refund against the PaymentIntent or Charge, and if you omit the amount you refund it in full, while passing a smaller amount (in the smallest currency unit, e.g. cents) issues a PARTIAL refund — you validate that a partial amount is positive and no larger than the original charge. A CANCELLATION ends the subscription, moving its status to canceled and stopping future invoices. Each produces a webhook — charge.refunded and customer.subscription.deleted respectively. The ACCESS half is entirely separate: neither Stripe event, on its own, removes your application's entitlements, because Stripe manages billing, not your feature flags. So the correct pattern is explicitly two-step: perform the money action, then, in your verified idempotent webhook handler, run the entitlement-revocation logic (flip the subscription/entitlement state so the resolver from earlier this module now denies access). Keeping these distinct also lets them diverge intentionally — e.g. a goodwill partial refund that does NOT revoke access, or a cancellation at period end that revokes only when the paid period actually ends. Model money and access as two decisions you make on purpose.

storyboard.say: Ending a paid relationship starts here: the customer wants a refund or a cancellation, and you trigger step one.

Here is the trap: that event moved money but did NOT touch access. If you stop here, the customer keeps full entitlements.
Step two is yours to handle: on the event, your webhook fires the access half and revokes the customer's entitlements.
Revoking entitlements flips application state so access is actually removed — the second, independent action completes.
The insight: money and access are two separate steps. Ship both — reverse the charge, then revoke on the event.

capstone-signup-pay-access.proof: An end-to-end pipeline that authenticates, verifies the webhook signature, dedups the event, updates subscription state, resolves entitlements, and gates a feature — reporting the final access decision.

capstone-signup-pay-access.text: Every lesson built one primitive: the auth gate, the signed webhook, the idempotency ledger, the state machine, the entitlement resolver. Production needs them working TOGETHER — a signup, a payment, a verified event applied exactly once, and a feature correctly gated. This capstone wires them into one path and proves the whole is correct.

A real "unlock on payment" flow is a small pipeline. A user AUTHENTICATES (Module 1). They pay via hosted Checkout (Module 2). Stripe sends a webhook that you VERIFY by HMAC signature (Module 3) and process IDEMPOTENTLY (Module 3), updating the subscription STATE (Module 3). Your ENTITLEMENT resolver (Module 5) then derives feature access from that state (Module 4). Finally a request for a feature is GATED on the entitlement. This capstone composes those primitives and runs a scripted scenario — including a replayed webhook — to prove the composition is secure and exactly-once.

The capstone is not new material — it is the correct, secure COMPOSITION of these into one path.

capstone-signup-pay-access.intro: The unlock pipeline as a sequence over the course primitives, ending in a gated feature.
steps: Authenticate first — an unauthenticated request never reaches billing logic.
Verify the webhook HMAC signature before trusting the event.
Dedup by event id so a replay applies the state change exactly once.

capstone-signup-pay-access.commonMistake: Wiring the primitives but skipping one guard under composition — e.g. resolving entitlements from an UNVERIFIED event, so a forged webhook grants access. The capstone must keep every guard on the one path.

capstone-signup-pay-access.text: Everything the course taught converges into one path, and the discipline is SECURE COMPOSITION — no guard dropped when the pieces are wired together. Model the flow as a pipeline. AUTHENTICATE the user (Module 1); an unauthenticated caller is rejected before anything else. Take payment with hosted CHECKOUT (Module 2), keeping card data off your server. When Stripe's webhook arrives, VERIFY its HMAC-SHA256 signature over timestamp.rawBody (Module 3) — an unverified event is untrusted and must not drive state. Process it IDEMPOTENTLY by event id (Module 3) so a redelivery applies the change exactly once. Apply the event to the subscription STATE machine (Module 3) and keep it honest with reconciliation. Then RESOLVE ENTITLEMENTS from the live plan+status (Modules 4–5) and GATE the requested feature on the result. Each stage is a primitive you built and tested alone; the capstone proves they fit together without a gap — the forged event is rejected at verification, the replay is absorbed by idempotency, the wrong plan is denied at entitlement. The output is a single access decision with a reason, which is the "proof, not vibes" artifact for the whole course: a real signup-to-access round trip where security holds at every seam. Build features this way — an explicit pipeline of guarded steps you can each defend — not as a hopeful chain of happy-path calls.

capstone-signup-pay-access.subtitle: authenticate → checkout → verify → dedup → state → entitle → gate

storyboard.say: The flow starts at the gate: authenticate the user first, because an unauthenticated caller must be rejected before anything else runs.
Once authed, we hand off to Stripe's hosted Checkout so card data never touches your server.
When payment completes, Stripe fires a webhook back to us — that event is the trigger for everything downstream.
The critical guard: verify the HMAC-SHA256 signature over timestamp and raw body. An unverified event is untrusted and must not drive state.
A genuine event flows to idempotent apply, keyed by event id, so a Stripe redelivery lands the change exactly once.
With state applied once, the entitlement resolver derives what this account is actually allowed to access.
Finally the feature gate reads those entitlements to allow or deny each request — the payment is now a real unlock.
The lesson: secure composition — every primitive stays guarded end to end, so no check is dropped when the pieces are wired together.

capstone-signup-pay-access.symptom: The composed unlock flow grants access from a forged webhook — an attacker POSTs a fake "active" event and gets features.

optionA.text: Assemble auth, verify, dedup, state, entitlement — each tested alone — into the pipeline. Every guard is defendable and reusable; the capstone is just wiring.
optionA.label: Compose primitives

optionB.text: Write it all in one function. Fewer files, but the guards tangle, you cannot test them in isolation, and it is easy to skip one (e.g. verification) under the tangle.
optionB.label: One inline handler

capstone-signup-pay-access.guidance: Compose (A). The course built each primitive alone precisely so the capstone is secure wiring, not new logic — which is what makes each guard testable and hard to accidentally drop. The monolith (B) is exactly how the "unverified event grants access" bug slips in.
